meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas. doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.title: mTOR-dependent synapse formation underlies the rapid antidepressant effects of NMDA antagonists
data.authors: Li N; Duman RS et al.

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Ketamine's rapid antidepressant action requires mTOR-dependent synaptogenesis in prefrontal cortex.
data.abstract_excerpt: The rapid antidepressant response after ketamine administration in treatment-resistant depressed patients suggests a possible new approach for treating mood disorders compared to the weeks or months required for standard medications. However, the mechanisms underlying this action of ketamine [a glutamate N-methyl-D-aspartic acid (NMDA) receptor antagonist] have not been identified.

extracted_findings.effect: mTOR-dependent synapse formation underlies the rapid antidepressant effects of NMDA antagonists (ketamine)
extracted_findings.dose: Ketamine 5-10 mg/kg (systemic); Ro 25-6981 10 mg/kg (systemic); Rapamycin, U0126, LY294002 (ICV infusion)
extracted_findings.effect_size: Ketamine (5-10 mg/kg) rapidly activated mTOR signaling, increased synaptic proteins (PSD95, GluR1, synapsin I), increased spine density, significantly increased EPSC frequency and amplitude, and produced rapid antidepressant effects in FST, LH, and NSFT. These effects were blocked by rapamycin. Ro 25-6981 (10 mg/kg) showed similar effects.
extracted_findings.limitations: The mechanisms underlying the induction of mTOR signaling are unclear. Ketamine is a psychotomimetic drug with abuse potential, and a more selective agent would be desirable for clinical antidepressant use.
